typeName: Q2: Analyze and interpret quantitative data
title: Age structure and survival in Countries P and Q

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using the population pyramids, describe the shape of each country’s age structure diagram, including data from the figure.

rubric.point: Describes Country P as having a wide base that narrows quickly with age, with a value from the figure.
accept: Country P has its largest cohort at ages 0-14 (about 9.0 million males and 8.8 million females) and each older cohort is smaller
a pyramid with a wide base

rubric.point: Describes Country Q as column-shaped or with a base narrower than the middle, with a value from the figure.
accept: Country Q has about 3 million of each sex at ages 0-14 and about 3.6 to 3.7 million at ages 45-59
bars about equal in width, slightly narrower at the base

parts.sample: Country P’s pyramid has a wide base: about 9.0 million males and 8.8 million females are 0 to 14, and each older group is smaller, down to 0.3 and 0.4 million aged 75 and over. Country Q’s diagram is close to a column, with about 3.0 million males and 2.9 million females aged 0 to 14 and slightly more, 3.6 and 3.7 million, aged 45 to 59.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Make a claim about which country’s population is likely to grow faster over the next 30 years, and justify your claim with data from the figure.

rubric.point: Claims that Country P will grow faster.
accept: Country P
P will grow faster than Q

rubric.point: Justifies with data: Country P has a much larger share of young people who will soon have children.
accept: about 17.8 million of Country P’s 48.3 million people (about 37%) are 0-14, compared with 5.9 of 37.0 million (about 16%) in Country Q
P’s 0-14 cohort is about three times Q’s

parts.sample: Country P will grow faster. About 17.8 million of its 48.3 million people (about 37%) are under 15, compared with 5.9 million of 37.0 million (about 16%) in Country Q. These young people will soon reach child-bearing age, so Country P will have many more new parents and births.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the survivorship table, (i) calculate the percent of babies in Country P who die before age 1, and (ii) identify which country’s survivorship is closer to a Type I curve and describe the evidence.

accept: 60 of 1,000 die before age 1, which is 6%
Country Q
Q is closer to Type I

rubric.point: (ii) Describes evidence: in Country Q most people survive to old age (960 of 1,000 at age 45, 640 at age 75) and deaths are concentrated late in life.
accept: Q keeps 992 at age 15 and 960 at age 45, compared with 880 and 700 in P
Q’s survivors drop mainly after age 45

parts.sample: (i) (1,000 - 940) / 1,000 × 100 = 6% of babies in Country P die before age 1. (ii) Country Q is closer to Type I: 992 of 1,000 are still alive at 15 and 960 at 45, and most deaths come after 45 (640 left at 75). Country P loses many more people at younger ages (880 at 15, 700 at 45).

mistakes.why: That is the percent that survive to age 1 (94%). The question asks how many die: (1000 - 940) / 1000 × 100.
Divide by the number born, 1,000, not by the survivors.
That is the percent that survive. 100% - 94% = 6% die before age 1.
That is the number per 1,000. Divide by 1,000 and multiply by 100: 6%.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Country P is improving clean water and vaccines for children. Explain how a fall in infant mortality is likely to affect Country P’s total fertility rate over the following decades.

rubric.point: States that the total fertility rate is likely to decrease.
accept: TFR will decrease
families will have fewer children

rubric.point: Explains the mechanism: when more children survive, parents need fewer births to raise the number of children they want.
accept: parents no longer need to have extra children to make sure some survive
as child survival becomes reliable, families choose to have fewer children

parts.sample: Country P’s total fertility rate is likely to decrease. When fewer babies die, parents can be confident their children will survive to adulthood, so they no longer need extra births to make sure some children live, and families choose to have fewer children.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Describe one likely economic or social consequence of Country Q’s age structure over the next 20 years.

rubric.point: Describes a consequence linked to Q’s large older cohorts or small young cohorts.
accept: more people will retire than enter the workforce, so fewer workers support more retirees through taxes
greater demand for health care and elder care
schools close or merge as there are fewer children
labor shortages that may be filled by immigration

parts.sample: Country Q’s large 45 to 59 age groups will retire within 20 years while smaller groups replace them, so there will be fewer workers paying taxes to support pensions and health care for a growing number of older people.
